1. Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (Graves' orbitopathy), euthyroid or subclinical variant — Most likely given bilateral, painless, gradual proptosis and 3 months of blurred vision; normal single TSH does not exclude TAO. Recommend: thyroid autoantibodies (TSH‑receptor antibody/TSI), repeat TSH with free T4/T3, orbital CT or MRI with contrast (look for fusiform extraocular muscle enlargement with tendon sparing), urgent ophthalmology exam (visual acuity, color vision, visual fields, intraocular pressure, EOMs, exophthalmometry).

2. Orbital lymphoma (eg, extranodal marginal zone/MALT lymphoma) — Presents as painless, progressive, often bilateral proptosis over weeks–months. Recommend: orbital MRI/CT to localize lesion, consider image‑guided biopsy for histology/flow cytometry, staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET‑CT).

3. IgG4‑related orbital disease (including dacryoadenitis) — Can cause bilateral, subacute painless proptosis and lacrimal gland enlargement; may have normal thyroid tests. Recommend: serum IgG4 level, orbital imaging, and biopsy if imaging suggests lacrimal/soft‑tissue mass.

4. Orbital metastases (eg, breast, lung, prostate) — Can be bilateral and progressive; consider if history of malignancy or systemic symptoms. Recommend: orbital imaging and biopsy if lesion identified; targeted systemic imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET‑CT) and review oncologic history.

5. Chronic/indolent idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease (orbital pseudotumor) or other inflammatory orbital processes — Less likely because IOI is often painful/acute, but chronic painless variants occur. Recommend: orbital imaging, inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), and biopsy when imaging is non‑diagnostic.

Priority next steps (to confirm/rule out): orbital MRI or contrast CT of the orbits, TSH‑receptor antibody (TRAb/TSI) and repeat thyroid panel (TSH + free T4/T3), serum IgG4, and prompt ophthalmology referral for detailed eye exam.
